# 04 — Advanced Combinatorics

This chapter is the bridge from "know the formula" to *derive the formula under
contest pressure*.  It assumes factorials, binomial coefficients and elementary
inclusion--exclusion (IE).  Read it before group actions and generating functions.

## 1. Recognition map

| Wording in a statement | First model to try |
|---|---|
| every required property is present | IE over missing properties |
| exactly/at least `k` properties | binomial inversion or weighted IE |
| partition labelled objects into unlabeled nonempty groups | Stirling numbers of the second kind |
| cycles of a permutation | unsigned Stirling numbers of the first kind |
| recursively nested / balanced / plane tree | Catalan family |
| sum over all subsets with a statistic depending only on size | binomial transform |
| constraints are local but labels are global | combinatorial class + EGF |

Always write what one object is, what is labelled, and whether order matters.
Most wrong generating functions arise before any algebra is performed.

## 2. Inclusion--exclusion as a transform

For bad events \(E_1,\ldots,E_m\), attach a set \(B(x)\subseteq[m]\) of bad
properties to each object. Then

\[
  \mathbf 1[B(x)=\varnothing]=\sum_{S\subseteq B(x)}(-1)^{|S|}.
\]

Summing this identity over objects proves IE and is more robust than memorising
signs.  If \(f(S)\) counts objects having every bad property in \(S\), the answer
is \(\sum_S(-1)^{|S|}f(S)\). Symmetry often collapses \(2^m\) terms into
\(m+1\): if \(f(S)=g(|S|)\), use \(\sum_k(-1)^k{m\choose k}g(k)\).

### Exactly `r` satisfied conditions

Let \(a_j\) count objects satisfying exactly \(j\) conditions and let
\(b_k=\sum_{|S|=k}f(S)\). Double counting pairs `(object, chosen k true
conditions)` gives

\[
 b_k=\sum_{j\ge k}{j\choose k}a_j,
 \qquad
 a_r=\sum_{k\ge r}(-1)^{k-r}{k\choose r}b_k.
\]

This is binomial inversion. The common transforms
\(b_n=\sum_{k\le n}{n\choose k}a_k\) and
\(a_n=\sum_{k\le n}(-1)^{n-k}{n\choose k}b_k\) follow similarly.

## 3. Classical counting families

### Stirling numbers

\[
{n\brace k}=k{n-1\brace k}+{n-1\brace k-1},\qquad
{n\brack k}=(n-1){n-1\brack k}+{n-1\brack k-1}.
\]

The first recurrence puts label \(n\) into one of `k` blocks or makes a new
block. The second inserts it after one of `n-1` existing permutation elements,
or creates a new cycle. Useful closed transforms are

\[
 {n\brace k}=\frac1{k!}\sum_{i=0}^k(-1)^{k-i}{k\choose i}i^n,
 \quad x^{\overline n}=\sum_k {n\brack k}x^k.
\]

Bell numbers satisfy \(B_n=\sum_k{n\brace k}\).  Their EGF is
\(\exp(e^x-1)\): a partition is a labelled **set** of nonempty labelled sets.

### Catalan schema

A plane rooted binary object is empty or a root with an ordered pair of such
objects, so \(C(x)=1+xC(x)^2\). Hence

\[
C_n=\frac1{n+1}{2n\choose n},\qquad
C_{n+1}=\sum_{i=0}^n C_iC_{n-i}.
\]

Equivalent objects include Dyck paths, balanced parentheses, triangulations,
and binary-search-tree shapes. Do not apply Catalan merely because parentheses
appear: check that the first-return decomposition is independent.

### Integer partitions

For unlimited parts, mark total size:

\[
P(x)=\prod_{j\ge1}(1-x^j)^{-1}.
\]

Restricting parts to a set deletes factors; allowing each at most once changes
the factor to \(1+x^j\).  Euler's pentagonal recurrence computes all \(p(n)\)
in \(O(N\sqrt N)\):

\[
p(n)=\sum_{k\ge1}(-1)^{k-1}
\left(p(n-k(3k-1)/2)+p(n-k(3k+1)/2)\right).
\]

## 4. Fast transforms by factorial scaling

Many triangular sums become one convolution. For example,

\[
b_n=\sum_{k=0}^n {n\choose k}a_k
=n!\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{a_k}{k!}\frac1{(n-k)!}.
\]

Convolve \(A_k=a_k/k!\) and \(F_k=1/k!\), then multiply coefficient `n`
by `n!`. This is \(O(N\log N)\) with NTT. The formula requires all required
factorials to be invertible; normally use a prime modulus with \(N<p\).

Stirling columns can also be obtained by convolution from the explicit formula.
For all \({n\brace k}\) at one fixed `n`, convolve
\(A_i=(-1)^i/i!\) and \(B_i=i^n/i!\); the coefficient at `k` is
\({n\brace k}\).

## 5. Rook polynomial viewpoint

For permutations avoiding forbidden cells, place nonattacking rooks in the
forbidden board. If \(r_k\) is the number of ways to choose `k` mutually
compatible forbidden assignments, IE yields

\[
  \sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k r_k(n-k)!.
\]

Disconnected boards multiply rook polynomials. This turns some intimidating IE
into polynomial products over small components.

## 6. Pitfalls and a worked derivation

**Example: surjections.** Count functions `[n] -> [k]` using every target.
Choose `i` omitted targets and apply IE:
\(\sum_i(-1)^i{k\choose i}(k-i)^n=k!{n\brace k}\). This simultaneously
explains the Stirling explicit formula: a partition into `k` nonempty fibers,
then an ordering of the fibers.

Frequent bugs:

- confusing labelled blocks (`k! {n\brace k}`) with unlabeled blocks;
- dividing by `k!` when the modulus does not permit it;
- using a closed form whose range crosses the characteristic;
- performing IE over constraints although intersections are not easier;
- silently counting rotations/reflections as distinct (see chapter 05).
